items.exemplar:
A. Most Gilded Age leaders did nothing: committed to laissez-faire, presidents from Grant to McKinley treated the trusts as natural and beneficial.

B. When leaders did act, it was late and limited — the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) and Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) were passed but barely enforced against the great combinations.

C. Workers responded by organizing: the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor built national unions, and strikes like Homestead (1892) and Pullman (1894) shook the nation.
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE way American political leaders responded to rapid industrial growth in the late nineteenth century.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND such response.
C. Briefly explain ONE way American workers responded to rapid industrial growth in the same period.
items.stimulus: Historian Richard Hofstadter observed that in the Gilded Age 'the United States was the only great industrial society in which the government played almost no part in regulating business' — a laissez-faire order workers and reformers would spend decades challenging.
